summary: Adds a /search endpoint with a hardcoded Stripe key in config, and changes paging offsets on /items. Also downgrades lodash, loosens the Dockerfile, and edits the deploy script and CI workflow.

findings.title: Search query built from request input
findings.description: The search handler puts q from the query string straight into the SQL text with an f-string. Nothing escapes or binds q. Any caller of /search can inject SQL and read or change every table in items.db. Pass q to cur.execute as a bound parameter with a ? placeholder.
findings.suggested_change: cur.execute("SELECT id, name, price FROM items WHERE name = ?", (q,))
findings.problem: The search handler puts q from the query string straight into the SQL text with an f-string. Nothing escapes or binds q.
findings.consequence: Any caller of /search can inject SQL and read or change every table in items.db.
findings.fix: Pass q to cur.execute as a bound parameter with a ? placeholder.

findings.title: Stripe secret key committed to source
findings.description: The config module stores a Stripe API key as a literal string in the repository. Anyone with repo access can use the key to act on the Stripe account. The key stays in git history after removal. Revoke the key in Stripe and read it from an environment variable or secret store at runtime.
findings.problem: The config module stores a Stripe API key as a literal string in the repository.
findings.consequence: Anyone with repo access can use the key to act on the Stripe account. The key stays in git history after removal.
findings.fix: Revoke the key in Stripe and read it from an environment variable or secret store at runtime.

findings.title: Paging offset skips the first page
findings.description: The list handler now computes offset as page times PAGE_SIZE, so page 1 starts at row 20. The first 20 items are never returned. Users of /items never see the first page of items, and every page shows the next page's rows. Restore the offset to (page - 1) times PAGE_SIZE.
findings.problem: The list handler now computes offset as page times PAGE_SIZE, so page 1 starts at row 20. The first 20 items are never returned.
findings.consequence: Users of /items never see the first page of items, and every page shows the next page's rows.
findings.fix: Restore the offset to (page - 1) times PAGE_SIZE.

findings.title: Container now runs as root
findings.description: The change removed the useradd step and the USER 10001 line. The Flask process now runs as root inside the container. An attacker who exploits the app, such as through the search injection, gets root in the container. Restore the unprivileged app user and the USER 10001 instruction before CMD.
findings.problem: The change removed the useradd step and the USER 10001 line. The Flask process now runs as root inside the container.
findings.consequence: An attacker who exploits the app, such as through the search injection, gets root in the container.
findings.fix: Restore the unprivileged app user and the USER 10001 instruction before CMD.

findings.title: Lodash downgraded to a vulnerable release
findings.description: The change downgrades lodash from 4.18.1 to 4.17.15. That release has known command injection, prototype pollution and ReDoS flaws. Any front-end code that uses lodash becomes exposed to these published vulnerabilities again. Keep lodash at 4.18.1 or later in package.json and package-lock.json.
findings.problem: The change downgrades lodash from 4.18.1 to 4.17.15. That release has known command injection, prototype pollution and ReDoS flaws.
findings.consequence: Any front-end code that uses lodash becomes exposed to these published vulnerabilities again.
findings.fix: Keep lodash at 4.18.1 or later in package.json and package-lock.json.

findings.title: Pull request title expanded into shell script
findings.description: The new step puts the pull request title into the run script through expression interpolation. A crafted title becomes shell commands on the runner. Any pull request author can run arbitrary commands in the CI job. The read-only token limits the impact. Pass the title through an env variable and quote that variable in the script.
findings.problem: The new step puts the pull request title into the run script through expression interpolation. A crafted title becomes shell commands on the runner.
findings.consequence: Any pull request author can run arbitrary commands in the CI job. The read-only token limits the impact.
findings.fix: Pass the title through an env variable and quote that variable in the script.

findings.title: Apt install runs without the yes flag
findings.description: The build runs apt-get install curl without -y. Apt asks for confirmation whenever it must pull in extra packages. The image build aborts when apt needs confirmation, because the build has no input to answer it. Add -y and --no-install-recommends to the install command.
findings.suggested_change: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
findings.problem: The build runs apt-get install curl without -y. Apt asks for confirmation whenever it must pull in extra packages.
findings.consequence: The image build aborts when apt needs confirmation, because the build has no input to answer it.
findings.fix: Add -y and --no-install-recommends to the install command.

findings.title: Base image uses the floating latest tag
findings.description: The change swaps the pinned python 3.12.7 slim image for python:latest. The latest tag moves to new Python versions without warning. A future build can silently pick up a new Python version that the app and CI do not test. Pin the base image to the tested release tag again.
findings.problem: The change swaps the pinned python 3.12.7 slim image for python:latest. The latest tag moves to new Python versions without warning.
findings.consequence: A future build can silently pick up a new Python version that the app and CI do not test.
findings.fix: Pin the base image to the tested release tag again.

findings.title: Unquoted path in recursive delete
findings.description: The deploy script now passes DEPLOY_DIR to rm -rf without quotes. The shell splits a path that has spaces into separate arguments. With a path such as /srv/my app, the script deletes /srv/my and the local app folder. The real deploy folder survives. Quote the variable and keep the empty-value guard.
findings.problem: The deploy script now passes DEPLOY_DIR to rm -rf without quotes. The shell splits a path that has spaces into separate arguments.
findings.consequence: With a path such as /srv/my app, the script deletes /srv/my and the local app folder. The real deploy folder survives.
findings.fix: Quote the variable and keep the empty-value guard.

findings.title: Deploy loop parses ls output
findings.description: The loop now splits the output of ls on whitespace. It also prints bare names instead of full paths. A file name with spaces shows up as several bogus entries in the deploy log. Loop over the glob as the previous code did.
findings.problem: The loop now splits the output of ls on whitespace. It also prints bare names instead of full paths.
findings.consequence: A file name with spaces shows up as several bogus entries in the deploy log.
findings.fix: Loop over the glob as the previous code did.

findings.title: Changed behaviour has no covering test
findings.description: The repository has no tests for the new search endpoint or the changed paging offset in list_items. Regressions such as the offset error or the injection reach users without any test failing. Add tests for /search with a quote in q and for /items page 1 returning the first rows.
findings.problem: The repository has no tests for the new search endpoint or the changed paging offset in list_items.
findings.consequence: Regressions such as the offset error or the injection reach users without any test failing.
findings.fix: Add tests for /search with a quote in q and for /items page 1 returning the first rows.

candidate.message: Using variable interpolation `${{...}}` with `github` context data in a `run:` step could allow an attacker to inject their own code into the runner. This would allow them to steal secrets and code. `github` context data can have arbitrary user input and should be treated as untrusted. Instead, use an intermediate environment variable with `env:` to store the data and use the environment variable in the `run:` script. Be sure to use double-quotes the environment variable, like this: "$ENVVAR".

dropped.reason: This duplicates the finding raised for the pull request title in the same run step.

candidate.message: Avoiding SQL string concatenation: untrusted input concatenated with raw SQL query can result in SQL Injection. In order to execute raw query safely, prepared statement should be used. SQLAlchemy provides TextualSQL to easily used prepared statement with named parameters. For complex SQL composition, use SQL Expression Language or Schema Definition Language. In most cases, SQLAlchemy ORM will be a better option.

dropped.reason: The code uses the sqlite3 cursor, not SQLAlchemy. The injection is already raised as one finding.

candidate.message: Detected user input used to manually construct a SQL string. This is usually bad practice because manual construction could accidentally result in a SQL injection. An attacker could use a SQL injection to steal or modify contents of the database. Instead, use a parameterized query which is available by default in most database engines. Alternatively, consider using the Django object-relational mappers (ORM) instead of raw SQL queries.

dropped.reason: This is a Flask app, not Django. The same injection is already raised.

candidate.message: User-controlled data from a request is passed to 'execute()'. This could lead to a SQL injection and therefore protected information could be leaked. Instead, use django's QuerySets, which are built with query parameterization and therefore not vulnerable to sql injection. For example, you could use `Entry.objects.filter(date=2006)`.
